original_interpretation: SIA/BCG reported Amkor investing US$1.6 billion in a 200,000 square-metre advanced packaging facility in Vietnam, and Intel's facility in Costa Rica, as examples of emerging-market ATP growth.
evidence_found: "Other countries expected to grow ATP capacity include Vietnam 25, where Amkor is investing $1.6 billion in a 200,000 sq. meter advanced packaging facility, and Costa Rica with Intel's facility. 26" (SIA/BCG May 2024, PDF p. 20). Intel FY2025 10-K (SRC-0348, Business/Strategy and MD&A): "in 2025 we initiated the consolidation of our Costa Rican assembly and test operations into larger existing sites in Vietnam and Malaysia, which we expect to be completed by the end of 2026".
correction: The SIA/BCG passage is quoted accurately (page is p. 20). But the Costa Rica example is out of date: Intel's FY2025 10-K says it is consolidating its Costa Rica assembly and test operations into Vietnam and Malaysia by end-2026, so Intel Costa Rica is no longer an ATP growth example.
notes: claim_type 'estimate' is loose: these are reported investment announcements relayed by an industry body, not modelled figures.

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG listed early US advanced-packaging investments: Amkor US$2bn in Peoria (to package TSMC Arizona chips for Apple), Intel US$3.5bn at Rio Rancho, New Mexico, SK hynix about US$4bn in Indiana, and a planned Samsung facility in Texas.
evidence_found: "Amkor announced it would stand up a $2 billion facility in Peoria, Arizona, to package chips produced there by TSMC for Apple, and Intel will invest $3.5 billion in advanced packaging at its Rio Rancho, New Mexico, facility. SK Hynix plans to invest roughly $4 billion to build an advanced packaging facility in Indiana. Furthermore, Samsung is planning to construct an advanced packaging facility as part of a larger semiconductor ecosystem in Texas." (SIA/BCG May 2024, PDF p. 21)
notes: Accurate as a record of what SIA/BCG reported in May 2024. These are 2023-24 announcements; later changes to the projects' size or status were not checked here and should not be read into this claim. claim_type 'estimate' is loose (these are reported announcements).

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG noted that IDMs are beginning to package newer nodes in-house using chiplet assembly, blurring the line between fabrication and ATP.
evidence_found: "IDMs are beginning to adopt this technology to package newer nodes in-house, blurring the lines between fabrication and ATP." (SIA/BCG May 2024, PDF p. 21, sidebar 'Chiplets')

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG estimated ATP at about 6% of semiconductor industry value added in 2022, with ATP value added measured by installed capacity at facility location.
evidence_found: Exhibit 2 'Semiconductor industry value-added by activity and region, 2022 (%)': row "ATP 6%"; note: "Wafer fabrication and Assembly & testing based on installed capacity and geographic location of the facilities." Source line: "IPnest; Wolfe Research; Gartner; SEMI; BCG analysis" (SIA/BCG May 2024, PDF p. 10)
notes: Location correction: Exhibit 2 is on p. 10 of the PDF, not p. 4. The facility-location basis applies to the regional split of ATP; the 6% is the activity's share of global value added.

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG put back-end (ATP) materials at US$24 billion of a US$64 billion semiconductor materials market, with substrates and lead frames about half of back-end materials.
evidence_found: "The $64 billion semiconductor materials market comprises chemicals and materials used in the front- end ($40 billion) and back-end (ATP) ($24 billion) of the supply chain." ... "Similarly, substrates and lead frames comprise about half of the back- end market ($12.8 billion)" (SIA/BCG May 2024, PDF p. 18)
notes: Location correction: p. 18, not p. 19. Report year of the materials figures is not stated.

original_interpretation: The CHIPS Act ITSI Fund (US$500 million, run by the US State Department) aims to expand international assembly, test and packaging capacity; partnerships were announced with Panama, Costa Rica, Vietnam, Indonesia and the Philippines.
evidence_found: "The US State Department is responsible for implementing the $500 million ITSI Fund, established under the CHIPS Act, to expand and diversify downstream capacity in the Indo-Pacific and Western Hemisphere. A core objective is to promote 'the expansion of the international assembly, testing, and packaging capacity needed to diversify the global semiconductor supply chain.' 29 The US government has announced ITSI partnerships with Panama, Costa Rica, Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines" (SIA/BCG May 2024, PDF p. 23)
notes: Location correction: p. 23, not p. 22. The claim restates SIA/BCG's account of the programme; claim_type 'estimate' is loose. The partner list is as of May 2024.

original_interpretation: Malaysia's investment agency MIDA stated that Malaysia holds 13% of the global market for chip packaging, assembly and testing services.
evidence_found: "According to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority's report on February 18, Malaysia holds 13 per cent of the global market for chip packaging, assembly and testing services." (Malay Mail, 19 Apr 2024, reposted on mida.gov.my)
notes: This is Malay Mail citing a MIDA report. It is a government agency promoting its own country and gives no basis or year, so 'reported_claim' is the right type. Not independently corroborated.

original_interpretation: TSMC said advanced packaging (its back end, 'advanced packaging testing as a whole') contributed slightly over 10% of its revenue in 2025, about 8% in 2024, and is expected to reach a low-teens percentage in 2026.
evidence_found: Jeff Su (IR): "What was the revenue contribution of what we call the back end, which is advanced packaging testing as a whole in 2025." Wendell Huang (CFO): "the revenue contribution last year from advanced packaging is slightly over 10% (corrected by company after the call). It's about 8% in 2024. We expect it to grow faster than the corporate average, and account for low-teens % in 2026." (TSMC 4Q25 call transcript, 15 Jan 2026, p. 10)
notes: The 2026 figure is guidance, not an actual.

original_interpretation: TSMC guided a 2026 capital budget of US$52-56 billion, of which about 10-20% is for advanced packaging, testing, mask making and others; advanced packaging capex had historically been below about 10%.
evidence_found: "In 2026, we expect our capital budget to be between USD52 billion and USD56 billion ... about 10 to 20 percent will be spent for advanced packaging, testing, mask making and others (added by company after the call)." (p. 4); CFO: "And the CapEx, yes, you are right, in the past, it's about 10%, lower than 10%." (p. 10)
notes: On the same page, IR's Jeff Su said the 10-20% guidance is 'the same as last year', so the 'below about 10%' history is for earlier years, not 2025. The 10-20% bucket also covers testing, mask making and others, not advanced packaging alone.

original_interpretation: TSMC defines the Foundry 2.0 industry as all logic wafer manufacturing, packaging, testing, mask-making and others; it said this industry grew 16% in 2025 while TSMC's US-dollar revenue grew 35.9%.
evidence_found: "Concluding 2025, the foundry 2.0 industry, which we define as all logic wafer manufacturing, packaging, testing, mask-making and others, increased 16% year over year. ... TSMC's revenue increased 35.9% year over year in US dollar terms, outperforming the foundry 2.0 industry growth." (C.C. Wei, TSMC 4Q25 call, 15 Jan 2026, p. 5)

original_interpretation: TSMC's 2025 advanced-packaging revenue was probably above US$12 billion (slightly over 10% of US$122.4bn), which would exceed Amkor's entire 2025 revenue (US$6.7bn) and make TSMC one of the two largest back-end service providers by revenue alongside ASE.
evidence_found: TSMC 4Q25 call p. 3: "Our revenue increased 35.9% in US dollar terms to USD122 billion"; p. 10: advanced packaging "slightly over 10%" of revenue. ASE 20-F FY2025, Item 5 segment table: "Packaging 308,342.6 [NT$m] 9,829.2 [US$m] 47.8% Testing 71,900.2 2,292.0 11.1%". Recomputed: 10% x US$122.4bn = US$12.2bn; ASE packaging+testing = US$12.12bn at the 20-F convenience rate.
notes: The arithmetic holds. TSMC's back end (more than US$12.2bn) and ASE's packaging and testing (US$12.1bn) are roughly equal, so the ordering between the two is uncertain. Both are about 1.8x Amkor. The Amkor US$6.71bn figure (CLM-0236) was not re-opened here. TSMC's figure is a rounded share of revenue, not a reported segment.

original_interpretation: Because TSMC's Foundry 2.0 definition adds packaging and testing, the same back-end revenue (e.g. ASE's or Amkor's logic packaging) is counted both in OSAT rankings and in TSMC's Foundry 2.0 market, so OSAT and Foundry 2.0 totals must not be added together.
evidence_found: "the foundry 2.0 industry, which we define as all logic wafer manufacturing, packaging, testing, mask-making and others" (TSMC 4Q25 call, p. 5).
correction: The definition includes packaging and testing, so logic packaging and test done by OSATs is inside Foundry 2.0, and adding OSAT totals to Foundry 2.0 would double count. The claim says 'must not be added together', but that holds only for the logic part: memory packaging and test (e.g. Powertech) and OSAT EMS revenue fall outside a 'logic' definition. TSMC does not publish Foundry 2.0 components, so the size of the overlap is unknown.
notes: An interpretation; the premise was checked against the TSMC transcript.

original_interpretation: A Citigroup analyst on TSMC's 4Q25 call said TSMC would work more closely with OSAT partners on leading-edge advanced packaging; TSMC did not dispute this in its answer.
evidence_found: Laura Chen (Citigroup): "I also think that before we talk about that, we'll work more closely with OSAT partners on the leading edge advanced packaging. So, just wondering what kind of the process will be, the key expansion plan in the space." IR restated her question without any mention of OSATs; the CFO answered only on revenue share and capex; C.C. Wei (p. 11): "we are investing in areas in advanced packaging where our customers need." (TSMC 4Q25 call, pp. 10-11)
correction: The analyst's wording is garbled and it is unclear who 'we' refers to. TSMC's IR restatement dropped the OSAT point and no TSMC speaker addressed it. Saying 'TSMC did not dispute this' suggests TSMC tacitly agreed, which the transcript does not support. Treat this only as an analyst's passing remark, not as evidence of TSMC's plans with OSATs.

original_interpretation: JCET reported record 2025 revenue of RMB 38.87 billion, up 8.1% year on year, with profit before tax of RMB 1.74 billion.
evidence_found: "JCET reported record full-year revenue of RMB 38.87 billion in 2025, up 8.1% year-on-year. Profit before tax (PBT) totaled RMB 1.74 billion, up 5.4% year-on-year, and net profit attributable to shareholders reached RMB 1.57 billion." (JCET/PRNewswire release, Shanghai, 9 Apr 2026)
notes: The evidence was recorded as a paraphrase, but the verbatim text matches. Source is a company press release, so 'reported_claim' is right; the audited annual report itself was not opened.

original_interpretation: JCET reported revenue associated with advanced packaging of RMB 27 billion in 2025, roughly 70% of its total revenue.
evidence_found: "Revenue associated with advanced packaging reached RMB 27 billion, marking a new high." (JCET release, 9 Apr 2026). Recomputed share: 27 / 38.87 = 69.5%.
notes: 'Roughly 70%' is our arithmetic, not JCET's statement. JCET does not define 'revenue associated with advanced packaging', and the wording ('associated with') suggests a broad definition, so do not compare it with Yole-defined advanced packaging revenue.

original_interpretation: JCET operates manufacturing in China, South Korea and Singapore.
evidence_found: "With eight manufacturing facilities across China, Korea, and Singapore, we deliver efficient supply chain solutions" (JCET release, 9 Apr 2026, 'About JCET Group'); the release also names "JCET Automotive (Shanghai) Co., Ltd." and "JCET Microelectronics (Jiangyin) Co., Ltd."
notes: The release gives the count as eight manufacturing facilities.

original_interpretation: In March 2024 state-owned China Resources Group agreed to buy 22.5% of JCET for CNY 11.7 billion (about US$1.6bn) from sellers including the Big Fund and SMIC, becoming its controlling shareholder.
evidence_found: "State-owned conglomerate China Resources Group will invest CNY11.7 billion (USD1.6 billion) to acquire 22.5 percent equity in JCET Group and take control of the leading Chinese integrated circuit packaging and testing services provider." ... "Pan Shi Hong Kong, another subsidiary of China Resources, will pay CNY29 (USD4) per share to asset sellers, which include Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation and the China Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund, JCET said yesterday." (Yicai Global, Fan Xuehan, 27 Mar 2024)
notes: Supports the March 2024 agreement. The source is financial press relaying JCET's announcement, not the filing itself; 'fact' would be better supported by the SSE announcement. Deal completion was not checked here.

original_interpretation: Gartner projected the combined IC packaging and test service market (OSATs, foundries and IDMs) at US$53.3 billion in 2017, of which OSATs US$28.1 billion and IDM in-house packaging and test US$25.2 billion.
evidence_found: "In total, the combined IC-packaging and test service market, which includes OSATs, foundries and IDMs, is projected to reach $53.3 billion in 2017, up 7% from $49.8 billion in 2016, according to Gartner. Of that figure, the IDM's in-house packaging and test sector are projected to have a combined dollar value of $25.2 billion in 2017, up from $23.9 billion in 2016, according to Gartner. And in total, the OSAT's packaging and test revenue is projected to reach $28.1 billion in 2017, up from $25.9 billion in 2016" (Semiconductor Engineering, Mark LaPedus, 8 Feb 2017)
notes: This is a forecast made in Feb 2017. The article also gives 2016 actual-basis figures (US$49.8bn total, US$25.9bn OSAT, US$23.9bn IDM) that could replace the forecast in ratio work. The 2017 figures are old; for newer views see SIA/BCG (US$95bn ATP, CLM-1076) and DIGITIMES 2024 (CLM-1026).

original_interpretation: IDMs and foundries with in-house packaging also outsource a portion of their packaging production to OSATs (dual sourcing).
evidence_found: "IDMs and foundries with internal packaging operations also outsource a certain percentage of their IC-packaging production to the OSATs. Generally, they don't have the capacity to produce everything." (Semiconductor Engineering, 8 Feb 2017)
notes: Misclassified: this is a journalist's descriptive statement, not a modelled figure, so claim_type 'estimate' is wrong. The AMD 10-K (SRC-0349) and Intel 10-K (SRC-0348) are primary-source examples of outsourcing and in-house mixes.

original_interpretation: Gartner Dataquest (mid-2000s) projected packaging, assembly and test revenue of US$48.16bn in 2007 with outsourced (SATS) revenue of US$21.1bn, and SATS reaching US$27.72bn of a US$59.12bn market in 2009, near parity with IDMs.
evidence_found: "Combined, total packaging and testing (PAT) revenues (IDMs plus SATS) will top $48.16 billion this year, up 8.9% from last year. Outsourcing revenues in the PAT market should do a little better, with about 10% growth to $21.1 billion."; "In 2008, Gartner sees a 12% increase in total worldwide PAT sales to $54.15 billion, followed by another minor slowdown to 9% growth in 2009 ($59.12 billion). SATS, meanwhile, will enjoy nearly 17% growth next year (to $24.53 billion) and 13% in 2009 (to $27.72 billion)."; SATS "is poised to balloon by nearly a third over the next three years and reach equal footing with IDMs." (Solid State Technology, James Montgomery, undated)
notes: The article has no date, but 'this year' is 2007 and it mentions SATS firms' soft 1Q07 and utilisation recovering after April, so it is mid-2007 (not 'mid-2000s' generally). All figures are Gartner Dataquest forecasts. Recomputed: SATS 2009 = 27.72/59.12 = 46.9%, not parity. 'Near parity' holds only loosely.

original_interpretation: Across published Gartner-based estimates, the outsourced share of assembly, packaging and test value rose from about 44% (2007 forecast) to about 52-53% by 2016-2019, and no public estimate shows a large change since then.
evidence_found: Recomputed from re-opened sources: 21.1/48.16 = 43.8% (Gartner Dataquest 2007 forecast, SST); 28.1/53.3 = 52.7% (Gartner 2017 forecast, Semiconductor Engineering); CSET 2019 28/53 = 52.8% (CLM-1037, verified). The researcher's own CLM-1117 computes 41.2/95 = 43% for 2024 (DIGITIMES OSAT revenue vs SIA/BCG ATP market).
correction: The ratios are arithmetically right, but every input is a forecast (2007, 2017), not an actual. The second half ('no public estimate shows a large change since then') is contradicted by the same research unit's CLM-1117, which shows about 43% for the mid-2020s from DIGITIMES and SIA/BCG. Restate as: outsourced share was about 44% (2007 forecast) and about 53% (2017 forecast, 2019 CSET); post-2019 public data give inconsistent pictures (about 43% if DIGITIMES 2024 OSAT revenue is set against SIA/BCG's US$95bn) because definitions differ.
notes: See the contradictions record with CLM-1117.

original_interpretation: Intel began consolidating its Costa Rica assembly and test operations into its other facilities, expected to be completed by the end of 2026, and discontinued its planned assembly and test expansion in Poland.
evidence_found: "We initiated the consolidation of our Costa Rican assembly and test operations into our other facilities, which we expect to be completed by the end of 2026, slowed the pace of construction for our new Ohio wafer fabrication facility, or fab, and discontinued planned expansions in Germany (fab) and Poland (assembly and test facility)." (Intel 10-K FY ended 27 Dec 2025, Item 1 Overview); elsewhere: "into larger existing sites in Vietnam and Malaysia".
notes: Intel's other facilities receiving the work are Vietnam and Malaysia.

original_interpretation: Intel states it predominantly manufactures its products in its own manufacturing and assembly and test facilities, supplemented by third-party suppliers.
evidence_found: "As a U.S.-based integrated design manufacturer, or IDM, ... [we] predominantly manufacture our semiconductor products at our manufacturing and assembly and test facilities, many of which are in the U.S."; "In recent years, however, we have also strategically utilized third-party foundry manufacturing capacity, including at one of our key foundry competitors, TSMC, for various tiles or an entire product" (Intel 10-K FY2025, Item 1).
correction: The 'predominantly' statement is verified verbatim. The 10-K describes the third-party supplement as foundry (wafer/tile) capacity, mainly TSMC. It does not describe outsourced assembly and test, so 'supplemented by third-party suppliers' should read 'supplemented by third-party foundry capacity (notably TSMC) for some tiles or products'.

original_interpretation: AMD sources assembly, test, mark and packaging from partners in Asia-Pacific: two ATMP joint ventures with Tongfu Microelectronics, plus SPIL (part of ASE) and KYEC.
evidence_found: "Wafers for our products are either sorted by the foundry or delivered by the foundry to our assembly, test, mark and packaging (ATMP) partners or subcontractors located in the Asia-Pacific region, who package and test our final semiconductor products. We are party to two ATMP joint ventures (collectively, the ATMP JVs) with Tongfu Microelectronics Co., Ltd. The ATMP JVs, Siliconware Precision Industries Ltd. (SPIL) and King Yuan Electronics Company (KYEC) provide ATMP services for our products." (AMD 10-K FY ended 27 Dec 2025, Item 1, p. 10)
notes: Risk factors (p. 22) add: "The majority of our ATMP services are provided by the ATMP JVs". The 10-K does not say SPIL is part of ASE; that is established by ASE's own 20-F, which lists SPIL subsidiaries.

original_interpretation: ITRI estimated Taiwan's IC packaging output at NT$423.3 billion (+7.7%) and IC testing output at NT$200.2 billion (+5%) in 2024, within total semiconductor output of NT$5.32 trillion.
evidence_found: "Taiwan's semiconductor industry output value exceeded NT$5 trillion for the first time in 2024, reaching NT$5.3151 trillion, an increase of 22.4%." ... "the IC packaging industry's output value will be NT$423.3 billion, an increase of 7.7%; and the IC testing industry's output value will be NT$200.2 billion, an increase of 5%." (Creating Nano Technologies site, 18 Feb 2025, machine-translated reprint of a CNA/TechNews report of 17 Feb 2025 citing ITRI IEK)
notes: Figures match (total NT$5.3151tn, rounded to 5.32). The source is a third-hand, machine-translated reprint on an equipment vendor's site (tier 3, correctly 'other'); the original CNA/TechNews or ITRI release would be stronger. The population note 'likely excludes foundry packaging' is the researcher's inference; ITRI's definition is not stated in the source.

original_interpretation: ITRI forecast (May 2025) Taiwan's 2025 IC packaging output at NT$461.5 billion (+9%) and IC testing output at NT$212.2 billion (+6%).
evidence_found: SRC-0351 (ocacnews.net) could not be re-opened: it returned an Incapsula bot block to both curl and the page tool. Alternate source (Asianet Newsable, 19 May 2025): "The IC packaging sector is projected to generate NTD 461.5 billion in 2025, up 9 per cent from a year ago. Similarly, the IC testing segment is expected to grow by 6 per cent to NTD 212.2 billion, according to ITRI data."
notes: Verified against an independent news republication of the same ITRI May 2025 forecast. It is a forecast. ITRI later raised its 2025 whole-industry estimate to NT$6.48 trillion (+22%) in Oct 2025 (CNA via creating-nanotech.com, 6 Nov 2025), so these segment forecasts are probably superseded. A search snippet attributes later 2025 figures of NT$480.3bn packaging (+13.5%) and NT$230.5bn testing (+15.2%) to ITRI, but I could not open that page (ocacnews.net/article/405790, bot-blocked), so it is not recorded as a claim.

original_interpretation: In Taiwan, testing is a large separate business: ITRI's figures put IC testing at roughly 32% of combined packaging-and-testing output in 2024 (NT$200.2bn of NT$623.5bn), reflecting independent test houses such as KYEC.
evidence_found: Recomputed from the re-opened ITRI figures (SRC-0350): 200.2 / (423.3 + 200.2) = 200.2 / 623.5 = 32.1%.
notes: The arithmetic is correct. 'Reflecting independent test houses such as KYEC' is interpretation; the source does not attribute the testing output to particular firms.

original_interpretation: ASE states in its 2025 20-F that it competes with independent packaging and testing companies, IDMs and EMS providers, and that some foundries have invested in advanced packaging capacity and won customers with it.
evidence_found: "We face competition from many sources, including other independent semiconductor packaging and testing companies, IDMs, and other EMS providers with large-scale manufacturing capabilities who can quickly react to market changes. In addition, some foundry players have actively invested and expanded their advanced packaging capacity and gained some customer bases with their services and solutions." (ASE 20-F FY2025, Item 3 Risk Factors, p. 8)

original_interpretation: ASE states that most of its customers obtain packaging and test services from more than one source.
evidence_found: "We face increasing competition, as most of our customers obtain services from more than one source." (ASE 20-F FY2025, Item 3 Risk Factors, pp. 8-9)
notes: Location correction: the sentence is in the Item 3 risk factor on competition, not in Item 4.

original_interpretation: ASE describes its testing operations and leading-edge advanced packaging as having relatively high fixed costs, making profitability depend on capacity utilisation.
evidence_found: "Our operations, in particular our testing operations and leading-edge advanced packaging, are characterized by relatively high fixed costs. ... Our profitability depends not only on the pricing levels for our services or products, but also on utilization rates for our machinery and equipment, commonly referred to as 'capacity utilization rates.'" (ASE 20-F FY2025, Item 3 Risk Factors)

original_interpretation: ASE states that demand for its advanced packaging and testing services is increasingly driven by customers developing AI processors, HPC chips and AI accelerators.
evidence_found: "The demand for our advanced packaging and testing services is increasingly driven by customers developing AI processors, HPC chips, and specialized AI accelerators." (ASE 20-F FY2025, Item 3 Risk Factors, p. 20)

original_interpretation: Setting DIGITIMES' 2024 OSAT revenue (US$41.2bn) against SIA/BCG's US$95bn ATP market implies OSATs perform only about 43% of back-end value, lower than the ~53% implied by Gartner 2017 and CSET 2019; the gap is likely definitional (SIA/BCG's total may value in-house and foundry advanced packaging generously) rather than evidence of insourcing.
evidence_found: Recomputed: 41.2 / 95 = 43.4%; 28.1 / 53.3 = 52.7%. SIA/BCG (May 2024, PDF p. 20): "The $95 billion ATP market is currently concentrated in Northeast Asia." No reference year is given for the US$95bn. DIGITIMES US$41.2bn (2024) is in verified CLM-1026.
correction: The arithmetic is correct, but the comparison mixes publishers, definitions and years: the SIA/BCG total is undated and includes IDM in-house facilities, and the Gartner 53% is a 2017 forecast. The 43% therefore does not show a decline in outsourcing, and the claim's own hedge ('likely definitional') is itself untested. Read it as: the implied outsourced share ranges from about 43% to 53% depending on which sources are combined.
notes: Conflicts with CLM-1104's 'no large change' statement; see the contradictions record.
